records.name: Kelantan
records.current_summary: Kelantan is the only sub-national unit in Malaysia — and in all of Southeast Asia — that has legislated the state of gender transition itself as a criminal offence. Clause 17 of the Kelantan Syariah Bill passed 12–13 August 2026 makes it an offence for a Muslim to change their own gender, cause another person's gender to be changed, or induce someone to do so, punishable by a fine up to RM3,000, imprisonment up to two years, or both; the Bill also adds 'protection of modesty' decency provisions. The predecessor provision was actually used: in a case reported February 2026, Kelantan recorded its first prosecution for gender transition under Section 18 of the Syariah Criminal Code Enactment (I) 2019 — a trans woman arrested by the state Islamic affairs department (Jaheaik) in an operation targeting a gathering of transgender individuals, heard at the Kota Bharu Syariah Court; the national monitoring group Justice for Sisters states Kelantan is the only state with such a provision. Critically, the Federal Court struck down 16 of 18 provisions of the 2019 Enactment on 9 February 2024 as outside state power; the Kelantan assembly resolved to re-enact them anyway, and did so in August 2026 — deliberate institutional commitment, not a stray provision. A foreign Muslim trans visitor is squarely within the Syariah jurisdiction; a non-Muslim visitor is technically outside it but still exposed to the official climate the sequence creates.

sources.claim: The Star (12 Aug 2026): previews the new Kelantan Syariah Bill replacing the 16 provisions of the 2019 Enactment the Federal Court struck down — including 'protection of modesty' clauses making it an offence for a Muslim to fail to safeguard their private parts (whipping of 3-6 strokes plus fine up to RM5,000 or up to three years) alongside the clause criminalising gender change.

The Star (13 Aug 2026): reports the Kelantan assembly passing the strict new decency rules of the Syariah Bill — the enactment replacing the Federal Court–voided 2019 provisions, including the offence of gender change.

records.name: Terengganu
records.current_summary: In May 2025 the Kuala Terengganu authority installed warning signboards about homosexual practice at several strategic locations in the state, framing homosexuality as 'dirty'; when criticised, state exco member Datuk Wan Sukairi Wan Abdullah confirmed the aim was deliberate — the boards were meant 'to instil hatred towards such acts among the community.' Justice for Sisters and twelve other civil-society organisations demanded removal on 14 May 2025 as a human-rights violation, so the record combines an explicit official statement of hostile intent with a documented civil-society counterweight. Terengganu additionally maintains a Hudud & Qisas Enactment 2002 that is unenforceable because of the federal Act 355 penalty cap — an aspirational legal ceiling the state nonetheless keeps legislating on, having amended its Takzir provisions from December 2022. What a visitor encounters is visible, ongoing, official hostility: signboards at strategic locations broadcasting that the state's stated purpose is to generate hatred; there is no criminalisation of trans status per se (contrast Kelantan), but the atmosphere is explicitly and officially manufactured.

sources.claim: The Star (10 May 2025): Terengganu exco member Wan Shukri defends anti-homosexuality warning signboards — installed near Universiti Malaysia Terengganu and other youth-frequented areas deliberately as a 'constant reminder' — confirming the purpose is to educate away from homosexuality; transgender activist Nisha Ayub condemns the move as institutionalised discrimination.

Malay Mail (14 May 2025): Justice for Sisters and 12 other civil-society organisations urge the Kuala Terengganu City Council to immediately remove the anti-LGBT signboards, calling them discriminatory hate speech under international human-rights law and condemning the exco member's defence as inciting hatred.

records.name: Kedah
records.current_summary: On 27 October 2020 the Kedah Islamic Department raided a birthday party at which 30 transgender women — singled out from approximately 100 attendees — were served notice to report to the state religious department for investigation under the Kedah Shariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1988; the event organiser was separately probed for 'encouraging vice,' which rights groups publicly condemned. The raid's design — isolating trans women as a category while ignoring the rest of the party — demonstrates that the state enforcement apparatus functions to process transgender people specifically. For a visitor present at or near such an event the risk is immediate: detention, investigation and prosecution under the 1988 Enactment. The incident is from 2020 and the instrument is an older state statute, but it evidences active, large-scale, category-targeted enforcement capacity and willingness in Kedah.

sources.claim: Malay Mail (30 Oct 2020): a coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups expresses concern over the probe of a Kedah event organiser for 'encouraging vice' after a private birthday party was raided and 30 trans women singled out and arrested — highlighting a trend of punishing organisers and allies of transgender persons.

records.name: Bali
records.current_summary: Bali offers the closest approximation to pockets of refuge in Indonesia: LGBTIQ+ people migrate there to "remake the meaning of home" and find spaces where they feel "valued, accepted and able to be themselves, even if those spaces are hidden and limited." No local enforcement actions, discriminatory bylaws, mass raids, or violence waves have been documented against trans visitors. The island sits outside OutRight's eight-province discriminatory-regulation set. However, the 2026 KUHP applies equally: Art. 412 criminalises sex outside marriage and cohabitation (up to one year, complaint-based by spouse/parent/child), and broad "indecency" provisions remain; travel guides advise discretion with public displays of affection for all couples. A 2025 ethnographic study of transpuan communities in Bali explicitly challenges the "romanticised refuge" framing, documenting "resistance and misrecognition" and systemic discrimination even there.  The deviation above the national score reflects absent local enforcement rather than a legal exemption. Materially safer than Jakarta (0.12) with its hotel raids and discriminatory regs, but not a protected space; the new KUHP and Perpres 111/2025 create fresh exposure that could be activated in any police contact.

sources.claim: Berghahn journal article (Anthropology & Medicine, 2025), an ethnographic study of transpuan (trans woman) communities in Bali: deliberately challenges the romanticised "refuge" framing, documenting persistent resistance and misrecognition and systemic discrimination on the island.

LGBTQ+ travel guide for Bali: flags same-sex relations criminalised under the new national penal code with "Exercise Significant Caution" advisory; frames the island as asking couples to keep affection quieter; notes Seminyak, Canggu, Ubud as the consistently gay-friendly areas.

March 2026 travel guide: "Bali is broadly welcoming to LGBTQ+ travellers... 'live and let live'" but the 2026 KUHP adds nuance; same-sex marriage not recognised; public displays of affection discouraged for all couples under conservative norms; no criminal enforcement recorded against tourists.

flags: 'No local enforcement actions, discriminatory bylaws, mass raids, or violence waves' — CONTRADICTED inside the project's own corpus: the Harvard Crimson article (cited in nine sibling province records) documents a trans woman's death in Bali custody in 2022
'remake the meaning of home' / 'valued, accepted and able to be themselves' — quoted solely from the never-fetched Multatuli page; absent from the cached Berghahn study

records.name: Papua
records.current_summary: No trans-specific incident series was found for Papua, but the dossier documents 138 recorded acts of torture or other ill-treatment in detention committed by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and Q1 2025, "with almost no consequences"; most victims were young men, several minors, arrested chiefly for alleged links to armed groups or protest participation. Named arbitrary-detention cases include three Papuans detained by officers at Nop Goliat Airport, Dekai (Yahukimo) on 26 July 2025 as two of them were preparing to depart for Jayapura to continue their studies. Q3 2025 saw a notable increase in military deployments and operations in the highlands, causing further internal displacement. For any visitor, including a transgender one, the probability that police contact escalates into unlawful detention and ill-treatment is documented and far above the national average. This is an amplifier finding on non-trans-specific evidence, not an independent conclusion about trans people.  It sits at the same level as West Sumatra (0.11) in deviation from the national score, though the mechanism differs: West Sumatra has an enacted bylaw with specified administrative penalties; Papua has a documented torture-and-arrest pattern that raises the severity of any encounter with security forces, without a trans-specific legal basis being needed.

sources.claim: TAPOL briefing (July 2025): police and military in West Papua committed 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands (Sept 2021-Q1 2025) with almost no consequences; victims mostly males under 24 plus 7 women and 7 minors; arrests largely for alleged armed-group links or demonstrations; deaths during torture documented in operation areas; incidents catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database.

HRM Papua quarterly report Q3 2025 ('Justice Denied'): notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025, further internal displacement, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions, and failure of accountability mechanisms.

flags: '138 recorded acts of torture... in Maybrat and the Central Highlands' — cited sources cover West Papua and Papua Highlands provinces, not Papua; and general conflict violence, not a trans visitor mechanism

records.name: Aguascalientes
records.current_summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score. The dossier's only Aguascalientes-specific findings are resident-facing: Human Rights Watch (March 2025) lists it among states that have not reformed their legislation at all to create a legal gender recognition procedure, and it has no enacted state-level non-discrimination protection on sexual orientation or gender identity (a February 2025 initiative was still only an initiative). No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found.

records.name: Campeche
records.current_summary: No criminalisation of trans presence. The state congress passed a 2024 reform amending the Civil Code to create an administrative legal gender recognition procedure, and Campeche's legislature recognises the transfemicide offence. No dedicated incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found; visitor-facing risk tracks the national baseline.

For Campeche: a 2024 Civil Code reform created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure.

Baseline for how a non-reforming state behaves.

records.name: Chiapas
records.current_summary: Same-sex conduct is legal and no law targets trans presence, but Chiapas is one of six states whose legislature has refused to create any legal gender recognition procedure (Human Rights Watch, March 2025). The practical consequence is permanently mismatched identity documents for trans people - the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in Mexico, since document mismatch is what triggers questioning at checkpoints - with no local procedure to cure it; courts can order recognition case by case, and Chiapas' proximity to Tabasco (where HRW documented mistreatment of trans people in state institutions) indicates a conservative institutional climate. Worse than the national position on documents and machinery, with no dedicated violence signal of its own.

records.name: Chihuahua
records.current_summary: No criminalisation of trans presence and no state legislative reform on legal gender recognition as of March 2025, but the Civil Registry runs an administrative procedure built on a 2019 Supreme Court ruling that struck down the state civil code's judicial-process requirement. Chihuahua also appears repeatedly as one of the states where lethal violence against LGBT+ people concentrates: it is named in the dossier's violence-concentration list and recorded 6 victims in the 2021 national annual count (19 of 32 states had victims that year). Mixed: functioning recognition machinery offset by a documented lethal-violence footprint.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024): documents how the absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure in Tabasco exposes trans people to police stops, denial of documents and institutional mistreatment - the country's clearest case of administrative erasure, cited to establish what a state without any procedure does to trans residents and visitors.
